title: Math is Exploring and Thinking
contentObjective: I can make sense of a problem, plan a strategy, and use fractions of a whole number to compare quantities.
languageObjective: I can explain my plan using the words we know, we don't know, and my strategy is ___ .

vocabulary.definition: An amount in a problem — a number with a meaning attached, like 540 meters.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una cantidad en un problema: un número con un significado, como 540 metros.
vocabulary.example: The heights of the buildings are the quantities in the problem.
vocabulary.visual: 540 meters — the number 540 AND what it measures.
vocabulary.cloze: A number with a meaning attached, like 540 meters, is a ___.

examples.why: A number together with what it counts.
Without a unit or a meaning it is only a number.

vocabulary.definition: How two quantities compare or connect to each other.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Cómo se comparan o se conectan dos cantidades entre sí.
vocabulary.example: Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel.
vocabulary.visual: 1 hour → 48 km, 2 hours → 96 km: as one grows, so does the other.
vocabulary.cloze: How two quantities connect or change together is a ___.

examples.why: One quantity responds when the other changes.

examples.text: A student's height and their house number
examples.why: Neither one moves because of the other.

vocabulary.definition: A plan for how to solve a problem before you start computing.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Un plan para resolver un problema antes de empezar a calcular.
vocabulary.example: We can think about how the quantities in the problem relate.
vocabulary.visual: “I will draw a tape diagram first, then divide” — chosen before computing.
vocabulary.cloze: The plan you choose before you start computing is your ___.

examples.text: Deciding to use compatible numbers to estimate first
examples.why: It is a plan chosen before doing the arithmetic.
The answer is the result, not the plan that produced it.

vocabulary.definition: A solution that makes sense in the context of the problem.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Una solución que tiene sentido en el contexto del problema.
vocabulary.example: A building that is 5/6 of 540 meters must be less than 540 meters.
vocabulary.visual: 5/6 of 540 must be under 540, so 450 is reasonable and 650 is not.
vocabulary.cloze: An answer that makes sense in the story of the problem is ___.

examples.why: You cannot wash part of a car, so the whole number fits the story.

examples.text: A discount that makes the sweater cost more
examples.why: It contradicts the situation, so it cannot be right.

vocabulary.definition: To keep working on a problem, checking your progress and adjusting your plan when you get stuck.
vocabulary.definitionEs: Seguir trabajando en un problema, revisando tu progreso y ajustando tu plan cuando te atascas.
vocabulary.example: When you hit a dead end, you try another strategy instead of quitting.
vocabulary.visual: Stuck on the tram problem → try a tape diagram instead → keep going.
vocabulary.cloze: To keep working and change your plan when you get stuck is to ___.

launch.narrative: Doing math is exploring: you make sense of a problem, plan a strategy, check your progress, and try new paths when you hit a dead end. Today's problems — walking distances and skyscraper heights — reward thinkers, not just calculators.

conceptIntro.heading: Make sense, plan, check
conceptIntro.intro: The book opens with two warm-ups: about how many peas are in the picture, and decompose 105.76 five different ways. Both are about thinking before computing.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Math Practices: Sense Making & Strategy Planning. 1. Identify known quantities and the unknown question. 2. Choose a strategy (draw a model, write an equation, or build a table). 3. Evaluate progress and pivot to an alternate approach if needed

iDo.title: Watch me estimate the peas
lines: A bowl is full of peas — far too many to count one at a time. About how many peas are in the bowl?
I do not count every pea — I look for a group I CAN count, like one small cluster of about 10.
Then I ask how many of those clusters would cover the whole bowl. I count about 12.
12 clusters of about 10 is 12 × 10 = 120, so my estimate is about 120 peas — a reasoned answer, close enough to be useful.
linesEs: Un tazón está lleno de chícharos — demasiados para contarlos uno por uno. ¿Aproximadamente cuántos chícharos hay en el tazón?
No cuento cada chícharo — busco un grupo que sí pueda contar, como un montoncito de unos 10.
Luego me pregunto cuántos de esos montoncitos cubrirían todo el tazón. Cuento unos 12.
12 montoncitos de unos 10 son 12 × 10 = 120, así que mi estimación es de unos 120 chícharos — una respuesta razonada, lo bastante cercana para ser útil.

weDo.title: Let's decompose 105.76 five ways
lines: Same number, five different breaks. Find one more of your own.
linesEs: El mismo número, cinco descomposiciones distintas. Halla una más por tu cuenta.

youDo.title: Now you try
lines: Three students walked different distances. Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel, and Evelyn walked a longer distance than Miguel.
Before computing anything, say what you KNOW and what you DON'T know — then pick possible distances for all three that fit the relationships.
linesEs: Tres estudiantes caminaron distancias distintas. Deon caminó una distancia más corta que Miguel, y Evelyn caminó una distancia más larga que Miguel.
Antes de calcular nada, di lo que sí sabes y lo que no sabes — y luego elige distancias posibles para los tres que cumplan esas relaciones.

conceptIntro.introEs: El libro abre con dos calentamientos: aproximadamente cuántos chícharos hay en la imagen, y descomponer 105.76 de cinco maneras distintas. Los dos tratan de pensar antes de calcular.
conceptIntro.keyIdeaEs: Prácticas matemáticas: comprensión y planeación de estrategias. 1. Identifica las cantidades conocidas y la pregunta desconocida. 2. Elige una estrategia (dibuja un modelo, escribe una ecuación o arma una tabla). 3. Evalúa tu avance y cambia de enfoque si hace falta

explore.instructions: The problem: Deon, Miguel, and Evelyn each walked a different distance through the neighborhood today. Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel. Evelyn walked a longer distance than Miguel. Nobody wrote down the exact number of miles anyone walked. — Making sense of a problem starts with separating what you know from what you do not. Sort each card, then tell a partner: can you still figure out who walked the shortest distance, even with no exact numbers?
explore.instructionsEs: El problema: Deon, Miguel y Evelyn caminaron cada uno una distancia distinta por el vecindario hoy. Deon caminó una distancia más corta que Miguel. Evelyn caminó una distancia más larga que Miguel. Nadie anotó el número exacto de millas que caminó cada quien. — Entender un problema empieza por separar lo que sabes de lo que no sabes. Clasifica cada tarjeta y luego dile a un compañero: ¿todavía puedes averiguar quién caminó la distancia más corta, aun sin números exactos?
explore.labelEs: Comparar caminatas: separa lo que el problema sí te dice de lo que no te dice.

discourse.prompt: Pick one card you put under 'We DON'T know this yet.' What would you have to figure out first to move it to the known column, and which quantity does it depend on?
discourse.sentenceFrame: To know ___, I first need ___, because ___ depends on it.
discourse.promptEs: Elige una tarjeta que pusiste en 'Todavía NO sabemos esto'. ¿Qué tendrías que averiguar primero para moverla a la columna de lo conocido, y de qué cantidad depende?
discourse.sentenceFrameEs: Para saber ___, primero necesito ___, porque ___ depende de eso.

connect.scenario: Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel, and Evelyn walked a longer distance than Miguel. You never learn the exact distances — but the relationships still tell you a lot.
connect.promptQuestion: How can you use the relationships among the distances to choose possible values for how far Deon, Miguel, and Evelyn walked?
connect.prompt: Pick a distance for Miguel. Then choose a distance for Deon that is ___ than Miguel's and a distance for Evelyn that is ___ than Miguel's, and explain how you ___ that your three values work.

check.stem: In the Comparing Walks problem, Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel, and Evelyn walked a longer distance than Miguel. Without any exact distances, what can you determine?
choices: The order from shortest to longest: Deon, Miguel, Evelyn
Nothing — you need exact numbers before you can compare
Deon and Evelyn walked the same distance
check.explanation: The two relationships alone place all three students in order — Deon below Miguel, Evelyn above Miguel — with no exact numbers needed; Evelyn walked LONGER than Miguel, not shorter.
check.stemEs: En el problema de comparar caminatas, Deon caminó una distancia más corta que Miguel, y Evelyn caminó una distancia más larga que Miguel. Sin ninguna distancia exacta, ¿qué puedes determinar?
check.explanationEs: Las dos relaciones por sí solas ponen a los tres estudiantes en orden — Deon por debajo de Miguel, Evelyn por encima de Miguel — sin necesidad de números exactos; Evelyn caminó más que Miguel, no menos.
choicesEs: El orden de la más corta a la más larga: Deon, Miguel, Evelyn
Nada — necesitas números exactos antes de poder comparar
Deon y Evelyn caminaron la misma distancia
Evelyn caminó la distancia más corta

check.stem: A student picks Miguel = 2 miles, Deon = 2.5 miles, Evelyn = 1.5 miles. What is wrong with these values?
choices: Deon's distance is greater than Miguel's, which breaks “shorter than”
Nothing is wrong — any three distances work
Evelyn's distance is too small compared to Deon's
Miguel's distance must always be the smallest of the three
check.explanation: Deon must walk LESS than Miguel, but 2.5 > 2 — the student swapped Deon's and Evelyn's values, which is exactly the check the Connect task asks you to run.
check.stemEs: Un estudiante escoge Miguel = 2 millas, Deon = 2.5 millas, Evelyn = 1.5 millas. ¿Qué tienen de malo estos valores?
check.explanationEs: Deon debe caminar menos que Miguel, pero 2.5 > 2 — el estudiante intercambió los valores de Deon y Evelyn, que es exactamente la comprobación que pide la tarea de conexión.
choicesEs: La distancia de Deon es mayor que la de Miguel, lo que rompe el «más corta que»
No tienen nada de malo — cualesquiera tres distancias sirven
La distancia de Evelyn es demasiado pequeña comparada con la de Deon
La distancia de Miguel siempre debe ser la más pequeña de las tres

check.stem: Building height problem: which statement shows you are CHECKING your solution against the relationship in the problem?
choices: “5/6 is less than 1, so my answer for London should be less than 540 meters”
“My answer is 650 meters, and that seems like a big number so it's probably right”
“I don't need to check once I've multiplied”
“Since I used a fraction, the answer must be exact”
check.explanation: Checking means comparing your answer's reasonableness against the relationship in the problem — a fraction less than 1 must give a result less than 540 — not just judging whether a number looks big or trusting the operation alone.
check.stemEs: Problema de la altura del edificio: ¿qué afirmación muestra que estás comprobando tu solución contra la relación del problema?
check.explanationEs: Comprobar significa comparar qué tan razonable es tu respuesta contra la relación del problema — una fracción menor que 1 debe dar un resultado menor que 540 — no solo juzgar si un número se ve grande o confiar solo en la operación.
choicesEs: «5/6 es menor que 1, así que mi respuesta para Londres debe ser menor que 540 metros»
«Mi respuesta es 650 metros, y eso parece un número grande así que probablemente esté bien»
«No necesito comprobar una vez que ya multipliqué»
«Como usé una fracción, la respuesta debe ser exacta»

connect.modelAnswer: I let Miguel walk 2 miles. Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel, so I chose 1.5 miles for Deon. Evelyn walked a longer distance than Miguel, so I chose 2.5 miles for Evelyn. I checked both relationships: 1.5 < 2 and 2.5 > 2, so my values fit. Any values work as long as Deon's is less than Miguel's and Evelyn's is greater.
connect.promptEs: Escoge una distancia para Miguel. Luego escoge una distancia para Deon que sea ___ que la de Miguel y una distancia para Evelyn que sea ___ que la de Miguel, y explica cómo ___ que tus tres valores sirven.
connect.scenarioEs: Deon caminó una distancia más corta que Miguel, y Evelyn caminó una distancia más larga que Miguel. Nunca te dicen las distancias exactas — pero las relaciones te dicen mucho de todos modos.
connect.promptQuestionEs: ¿Cómo puedes usar las relaciones entre las distancias para escoger valores posibles de cuánto caminaron Deon, Miguel y Evelyn?
connect.modelAnswerEs: Puse que Miguel caminó 2 millas. Deon caminó una distancia más corta que Miguel, así que escogí 1.5 millas para Deon. Evelyn caminó una distancia más larga que Miguel, así que escogí 2.5 millas para Evelyn. Comprobé las dos relaciones: 1.5 < 2 y 2.5 > 2, así que mis valores sirven. Cualquier valor funciona mientras el de Deon sea menor que el de Miguel y el de Evelyn sea mayor.

approaching.stem: Which of these is a correct way to decompose 105.76?
approaching.explanation: 100 + 5.76 = 105.76. Decomposing means the parts must rebuild the original number exactly.
choiceFeedback: 100 + 5.076 = 105.076 — that pushes the digits one decimal place too far right.
105 + 7.6 = 112.6, not 105.76 — the 7 and 6 belong in the tenths and hundredths places.
10 + 5.76 = 15.76 — that drops the hundreds digit of 105.76.
hints: Add each option and compare to 105.76.
The parts must total 105.76 exactly.
Add the two parts in each choice. Only one total lands exactly on 105.76.
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cuál de estas es una manera correcta de descomponer 105.76?
approaching.explanationEs: 100 + 5.76 = 105.76. Descomponer significa que las partes deben reconstruir el número original exactamente.
hintsEs: Suma cada opción y compara con 105.76.
Las partes deben sumar exactamente 105.76.
Suma las dos partes de cada opción. Solo un total cae exactamente en 105.76.

approaching.stem: Which is another correct decomposition of 105.76?
approaching.explanation: 110 − 4.24 = 105.76. A decomposition can use subtraction, not only addition.
choiceFeedback: 110 − 5.24 = 104.76 — that takes away one whole too many.
106 − 0.34 = 105.66 — the difference from 106 is 0.24, not 0.34.
110 + 4.24 = 114.24 — that moves away from 105.76 instead of down to it.
hints: Start at 110. How far down is 105.76?
So subtracting 4.24 from 110 works.
approaching.explanationEs: 110 − 4.24 = 105.76. Una descomposición puede usar resta, no solo suma.
hintsEs: Empieza en 110. ¿Qué tanto hay que bajar hasta 105.76?
Así que restar 4.24 de 110 funciona.

approaching.stem: Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel, and Evelyn walked a longer distance than Miguel. Who walked the shortest distance?
approaching.explanation: Deon is below Miguel and Evelyn is above Miguel, so the order is Deon < Miguel < Evelyn — Deon walked the shortest distance.
choiceFeedback: Miguel is in the middle: Deon walked less than him and Evelyn walked more.
Evelyn walked a LONGER distance than Miguel, so she walked the most, not the least.
It can be determined — the two relationships put all three students in order even without exact numbers.
hints: Put Miguel in the middle and place the other two around him.
Deon is below Miguel; Evelyn is above Miguel.
Who ends up lowest?
approaching.stemEs: Deon caminó una distancia más corta que Miguel, y Evelyn caminó una distancia más larga que Miguel. ¿Quién caminó la distancia más corta?
approaching.explanationEs: Deon está por debajo de Miguel y Evelyn por encima de Miguel, así que el orden es Deon < Miguel < Evelyn — Deon caminó la distancia más corta.
hintsEs: Pon a Miguel en el medio y coloca a los otros dos alrededor de él.
Deon está por debajo de Miguel; Evelyn está por encima de Miguel.
¿Quién queda más abajo?

approaching.stem: In the Comparing Walks problem, name one thing you KNOW and one thing you DON'T know.
approaching.modelAnswer: I know that Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel. I don't know how far each student actually walked.
approaching.stemEs: En el problema de Comparar Caminatas, nombra una cosa que SABES y una que NO sabes.

approaching.stem: The London building will be 5/6 as tall as One World Trade Center, which is 540 meters. How tall will the London building be?
approaching.explanation: 5/6 × 540: one sixth of 540 is 90, and 5 sixths is 5 × 90 = 450 meters.
choiceFeedback: 90 meters is only 1/6 of 540 — you still need to multiply by the 5 in the numerator.
648 meters is 6/5 of 540 — that flips the fraction and makes the building taller than 540.
534 meters subtracts 6 from 540 instead of finding 5/6 OF 540.
hints: First find one sixth of 540.
Now take 5 of those sixths.
approaching.stemEs: El edificio de Londres será 5/6 de alto que el One World Trade Center, que mide 540 metros. ¿Qué altura tendrá el edificio de Londres?
approaching.explanationEs: 5/6 × 540: un sexto de 540 es 90, y 5 sextos son 5 × 90 = 450 metros.
hintsEs: Halla primero un sexto de 540.
Ahora toma 5 de esos sextos.

approaching.stem: What can you do if you're stuck on a problem?
approaching.modelAnswer: I can check that I have answered the question and that my solution makes sense, go back to what I know from the problem, or try a different strategy instead of giving up.
sentenceStems: Another strategy I could try is ___ .
approaching.stemEs: ¿Qué puedes hacer si te atoras en un problema?

approaching.instructions: Each new building is a fraction of One World Trade Center's 540 meters. Sort each plan without computing.
approaching.instructionsEs: Cada edificio nuevo es una fracción de los 540 metros del One World Trade Center. Clasifica cada plan sin calcular.
approaching.label: Sort each building plan: shorter or taller than 540 meters?
approaching.labelEs: Clasifica cada plan: ¿más bajo o más alto que 540 metros?

categories.label: Shorter than 540 m (fraction less than 1)
categories.labelEs: Más bajo que 540 m (fracción menor que 1)

categories.label: Taller than 540 m (fraction greater than 1)
categories.labelEs: Más alto que 540 m (fracción mayor que 1)

hints: Compare the numerator to the denominator before you multiply anything.
A fraction less than 1 shrinks the 540; a fraction greater than 1 stretches it.
hintsEs: Compara el numerador con el denominador antes de multiplicar nada.
Una fracción menor que 1 encoge los 540; una fracción mayor que 1 los estira.
approaching.explanation: No computation is needed: when the numerator is smaller than the denominator (9/10, 5/6, 3/4) the fraction is less than 1, so the building is shorter than 540 m. When the numerator is larger (6/5, 11/10, 7/6) the fraction is greater than 1, so the building is taller.
approaching.explanationEs: No hace falta calcular: cuando el numerador es menor que el denominador (9/10, 5/6, 3/4), la fracción es menor que 1 y el edificio es más bajo que 540 m. Cuando el numerador es mayor (6/5, 11/10, 7/6), la fracción es mayor que 1 y el edificio es más alto.

onLevel.stem: The Rio de Janeiro building will be 9/10 as tall as One World Trade Center (540 meters). How tall will it be?
onLevel.explanation: 9/10 × 540: one tenth of 540 is 54, and 9 tenths is 9 × 54 = 486 meters.
choiceFeedback: 54 meters is only 1/10 of 540 — you still need 9 of those tenths.
4,860 meters multiplies 540 by 9 but never divides by 10.
594 meters ADDS one tenth (540 + 54) instead of taking 9 tenths of 540.
hints: First find one tenth of 540.
Multiply that tenth by 9.
onLevel.stemEs: El edificio de Río de Janeiro será 9/10 de alto que el One World Trade Center (540 metros). ¿Qué altura tendrá?
onLevel.explanationEs: 9/10 × 540: un décimo de 540 es 54, y 9 décimos son 9 × 54 = 486 metros.
hintsEs: Halla primero un décimo de 540.
Multiplica ese décimo por 9.

onLevel.stem: The Tokyo building will be 6/5 as tall as One World Trade Center (540 meters). How tall will it be?
onLevel.explanation: 6/5 × 540: one fifth of 540 is 108, and 6 fifths is 6 × 108 = 648 meters — taller than 540, because 6/5 is greater than 1.
choiceFeedback: 450 meters is 5/6 of 540 — that flips the fraction, and it belongs to the London building.
108 meters is only 1/5 of 540 — you still need 6 of those fifths.
432 meters SUBTRACTS a fifth (540 − 108) instead of taking 6 fifths.
hints: First find one fifth of 540.
6/5 means six of those fifths — will that be more or less than 540?
onLevel.stemEs: El edificio de Tokio será 6/5 de alto que el One World Trade Center (540 metros). ¿Qué altura tendrá?
onLevel.explanationEs: 6/5 × 540: un quinto de 540 es 108, y 6 quintos son 6 × 108 = 648 metros — más alto que 540, porque 6/5 es mayor que 1.
hintsEs: Halla primero un quinto de 540.
6/5 significa seis de esos quintos — ¿eso será más o menos que 540?

onLevel.stem: Without calculating, which new building must be TALLER than One World Trade Center, and why?
choices: London, because 5/6 has a 6 in it
Rio de Janeiro, because 9/10 is close to 1
None — a fraction of 540 is always less than 540
onLevel.explanation: Multiplying 540 by a fraction greater than 1 gives more than 540. Only 6/5 is greater than 1; 5/6 and 9/10 are both less than 1.
choiceFeedback: The 6 in 5/6 is the denominator — 5/6 is less than 1, so the London building is SHORTER than 540 meters.
Close to 1 is not greater than 1 — 9/10 of 540 is still less than 540 meters.
A fraction GREATER than 1, like 6/5, makes the product greater than 540.
hints: Compare each fraction to 1.
Multiplying by a fraction greater than 1 makes the result bigger.
onLevel.stemEs: Sin calcular, ¿cuál edificio nuevo debe ser MÁS ALTO que el One World Trade Center, y por qué?
onLevel.explanationEs: Multiplicar 540 por una fracción mayor que 1 da más de 540. Solo 6/5 es mayor que 1; 5/6 y 9/10 son ambas menores que 1.
hintsEs: Compara cada fracción con 1.
Multiplicar por una fracción mayor que 1 hace el resultado más grande.

onLevel.stem: Suppose Miguel walked 2 miles. Choose possible distances for Deon and Evelyn that fit the problem, and explain how you checked them.
onLevel.modelAnswer: Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel, so Deon could have walked 1.5 miles. Evelyn walked a longer distance than Miguel, so Evelyn could have walked 2.5 miles. I checked: 1.5 < 2 and 2.5 > 2, so both relationships are true.
onLevel.stemEs: Supón que Miguel caminó 2 millas. Escoge distancias posibles para Deon y Evelyn que encajen con el problema, y explica cómo las revisaste.

onLevel.stem: You calculate 5/6 × 540 and get 650 meters. What does the checking step of your plan tell you?
choices: The answer is unreasonable — 5/6 of 540 must be LESS than 540
The answer is fine because it is close to 540
The answer is fine because 650 is a bigger number than 5/6
Checking is only needed when the problem asks for it
onLevel.explanation: 5/6 is less than 1, so 5/6 of 540 must land below 540. Getting 650 means the plan needs adjusting — which is exactly what checking is for.
choiceFeedback: Close to 540 is not the test — the answer must be BELOW 540, because 5/6 is less than 1.
Comparing 650 to the fraction 5/6 mixes up two different kinds of quantities — compare the answer to 540 instead.
This lesson says we check our progress on EVERY problem, not only when asked.
hints: Is 5/6 more or less than 1?
Multiplying by a fraction less than 1 makes the result smaller.
So should the answer be above or below 540?
onLevel.stemEs: Calculas 5/6 × 540 y obtienes 650 metros. ¿Qué te dice el paso de revisión de tu plan?
onLevel.explanationEs: 5/6 es menor que 1, así que 5/6 de 540 debe quedar por debajo de 540. Obtener 650 significa que hay que ajustar el plan — para eso sirve revisar.
hintsEs: ¿5/6 es más o menos que 1?
Multiplicar por una fracción menor que 1 hace el resultado más pequeño.
Entonces, ¿la respuesta debe estar arriba o abajo de 540?

onLevel.stem: The lesson says we check on our progress toward a solution and adjust our plan as needed. Describe one way YOU can check on your progress while solving a problem.
onLevel.modelAnswer: I can stop partway and ask whether my numbers still make sense in the story — for example, if a building is supposed to be a fraction less than 1 of 540 meters, my answer so far should be under 540. If it isn't, I go back and adjust my plan.
sentenceStems: One way I check my progress is ___ .
If something doesn't make sense, I ___ .
onLevel.stemEs: La lección dice que revisamos nuestro avance hacia una solución y ajustamos el plan cuando hace falta. Describe una manera en que TÚ puedes revisar tu avance mientras resuelves un problema.

onLevel.label: Compute each building's height as a fraction of 540 meters.
onLevel.labelEs: Calcula la altura de cada edificio como fracción de 540 metros.
hints: Divide 540 by the denominator first, then multiply by the numerator.
540 ÷ 10 = 54 and 540 ÷ 5 = 108 — both divide evenly, which is why these fractions are friendly.
hintsEs: Divide 540 entre el denominador primero y luego multiplica por el numerador.
540 ÷ 10 = 54 y 540 ÷ 5 = 108: ambos dividen exacto, por eso estas fracciones son amigables.
onLevel.explanation: For 9/10 of 540: 540 ÷ 10 = 54, then 54 × 9 = 486. For 6/5 of 540: 540 ÷ 5 = 108, then 108 × 6 = 648 — taller than the original, as a fraction greater than 1 predicts. Half of 540 is 270.
onLevel.explanationEs: Para 9/10 de 540: 540 ÷ 10 = 54, luego 54 × 9 = 486. Para 6/5 de 540: 540 ÷ 5 = 108, luego 108 × 6 = 648, más alto que el original, como predice una fracción mayor que 1. La mitad de 540 es 270.

extending.stem: Which set shows FIVE different correct decompositions of 105.76?
extending.explanation: All five in the first set rebuild 105.76 exactly — by addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division.
choiceFeedback: 105 + 7.6 = 112.6, so that set contains an error.
52.88 × 3 = 158.64, so that set contains an error.
hints: Check every member of each set.
One wrong member spoils the whole set.
Find the set where all five land exactly on 105.76.
extending.stemEs: ¿Cuál conjunto muestra CINCO descomposiciones correctas y distintas de 105.76?
extending.explanationEs: Las cinco del primer conjunto reconstruyen 105.76 exactamente — con suma, resta, multiplicación y división.
hintsEs: Revisa cada miembro de cada conjunto.
Un solo miembro incorrecto arruina todo el conjunto.
Halla el conjunto donde las cinco caen exactamente en 105.76.

extending.stem: Without computing the exact heights, order the three new buildings from shortest to tallest. (London: 5/6 of 540 m, Rio de Janeiro: 9/10 of 540 m, Tokyo: 6/5 of 540 m.)
extending.explanation: Compare the fractions: 5/6 ≈ 0.83 is less than 9/10 = 0.9, and both are less than 6/5 = 1.2. Same whole, so the order of the fractions is the order of the heights.
choiceFeedback: That puts 9/10 below 5/6 — but 9/10 = 0.9 is GREATER than 5/6 ≈ 0.83.
That is tallest to shortest — the question asks for shortest to tallest.
Tokyo's 6/5 is greater than 1, so Tokyo must be last, not in the middle.
hints: All three are fractions of the SAME 540 meters, so just compare the fractions.
Compare each fraction to 1, then compare 5/6 and 9/10 to each other.
extending.stemEs: Sin calcular las alturas exactas, ordena los tres edificios nuevos del más bajo al más alto. (Londres: 5/6 de 540 m, Río de Janeiro: 9/10 de 540 m, Tokio: 6/5 de 540 m.)
extending.explanationEs: Compara las fracciones: 5/6 ≈ 0.83 es menor que 9/10 = 0.9, y ambas son menores que 6/5 = 1.2. El mismo entero, así que el orden de las fracciones es el orden de las alturas.
hintsEs: Las tres son fracciones de los MISMOS 540 metros, así que solo compara las fracciones.
Compara cada fracción con 1, y luego compara 5/6 y 9/10 entre sí.

extending.stem: A classmate says, "In math, only the final answer matters." Using this lesson, write what you would say back.
extending.modelAnswer: I would say the thinking matters just as much. In the buildings problem we knew London and Rio would be under 540 meters and Tokyo would be over BEFORE calculating, because we compared the fractions to 1. That checking is what catches mistakes — when we do math, we make sense of problems, check our progress, and try other strategies at dead ends.
sentenceStems: One example from this lesson is ___ .
extending.stemEs: Un compañero dice: "En matemáticas, solo importa la respuesta final." Usando esta lección, escribe qué le responderías.

extending.stem: Write your own Comparing Walks problem: describe three people using only relationships (shorter than, longer than), so a reader can put them in order without any exact distances. Then give one set of values that fits.
extending.modelAnswer: Ava ran a shorter distance than Ben, and Cora ran a longer distance than Ben. The order must be Ava, then Ben, then Cora. One set of values that fits: Ava 3 km, Ben 4 km, Cora 5.5 km, because 3 < 4 and 5.5 > 4.
sentenceStems: ___ walked a shorter distance than ___ , and ___ walked a longer distance than ___ .
One set of values that fits is ___ because ___ .
extending.stemEs: Escribe tu propio problema de Comparar Caminatas: describe a tres personas usando solo relaciones (más corta que, más larga que), para que un lector pueda ordenarlas sin distancias exactas. Luego da un conjunto de valores que encaje.

extending.stem: Apply — City Blocks. A city block has 12 buildings. The block to the north is planned to hold 2/3 as many buildings, and the block to the east is planned to hold 3/2 as many. WITHOUT computing, say which block will hold the most buildings and how you know. Then find the number of buildings on each block and check that your answers make sense.
extending.modelAnswer: The east block will hold the most, because 3/2 is greater than 1 and the other fractions are less than 1 — and all three describe the same 12 buildings. North: 2/3 × 12 = 8 buildings. East: 3/2 × 12 = 18 buildings. The original block has 12. The answers make sense because 8 is less than 12 and 18 is more than 12, which is what the fractions predicted.
sentenceStems: The ___ block will hold the most because its fraction is ___ than 1.
I found ___ × 12 = ___ buildings, and that makes sense because ___.
extending.stemEs: Aplica — Cuadras de la ciudad. Una cuadra tiene 12 edificios. Se planea que la cuadra del norte tenga 2/3 de esa cantidad de edificios, y que la cuadra del este tenga 3/2 de esa cantidad. SIN calcular, di cuál cuadra tendrá más edificios y cómo lo sabes. Luego halla el número de edificios de cada cuadra y revisa que tus respuestas tengan sentido.

extending.label: Match each fraction of 540 to a shortcut that computes it.
extending.labelEs: Empareja cada fracción de 540 con un atajo que la calcula.
hints: 9/10 is one tenth LESS than the whole — so subtract one tenth of 540.
6/5 is one fifth MORE than the whole — so add one fifth of 540.
hintsEs: 9/10 es una décima MENOS que el total, así que resta una décima de 540.
6/5 es un quinto MÁS que el total, así que suma un quinto de 540.
extending.explanation: Each shortcut rewrites the fraction around the whole: 9/10 = 1 − 1/10, so subtract 54; 6/5 = 1 + 1/5, so add 108; 5/6 = 1 − 1/6, so subtract 90; and 1/2 is simply dividing by 2. Seeing fractions as 'the whole, adjusted' is the strategy-planning move of this lesson.
extending.explanationEs: Cada atajo reescribe la fracción alrededor del total: 9/10 = 1 − 1/10, así que resta 54; 6/5 = 1 + 1/5, así que suma 108; 5/6 = 1 − 1/6, así que resta 90; y 1/2 es simplemente dividir entre 2. Ver las fracciones como 'el total, ajustado' es la estrategia de esta lección.

practice.commonMistake: Expecting a fraction of a number to be bigger than the number — 5/6 × 540 must be LESS than 540 because 5/6 is less than 1; only a fraction greater than 1, like 6/5, makes the product bigger.

diagram.title: Two ways to reach 105.76
diagram.caption: Decompose by building up from 100 or by backing down from 110 — both land on the same point

exitTicket.stem: Which statement best shows what this lesson means by "math is exploring and thinking"?
choices: We make sense of problems, plan a strategy, check our progress, and try other strategies at dead ends
We compute as fast as possible and move on to the next problem
We wait for someone to show us the one correct method
We only check our work when the answer looks wrong
exitTicket.explanation: The summary names the whole cycle: make sense of the problem, develop a plan, check progress and adjust, and make sense of the solution in context.
hints: Look back at the Summarize slide.
It describes a cycle, not a single step.
Which option includes making sense, planning, AND checking?
exitTicket.stemEs: ¿Qué afirmación muestra mejor lo que esta lección quiere decir con «las matemáticas son explorar y pensar»?
choicesEs: Entendemos los problemas, planeamos una estrategia, revisamos nuestro avance y probamos otras estrategias cuando nos atoramos
Calculamos lo más rápido posible y pasamos al siguiente problema
Esperamos a que alguien nos muestre el único método correcto
Solo revisamos nuestro trabajo cuando la respuesta se ve mal
exitTicket.explanationEs: El resumen nombra el ciclo completo: entender el problema, desarrollar un plan, revisar el avance y ajustar, y darle sentido a la solución en su contexto.
hintsEs: Vuelve a mirar la diapositiva de resumen.
Describe un ciclo, no un solo paso.
¿Qué opción incluye entender, planear y revisar?

turnAndTalk.question: The book decomposes 105.76 as one example: 100 + 5.76. Why must the parts of a decomposition always rebuild the original number exactly?
turnAndTalk.kernel: The lesson's warm-up decomposes 105.76 several different ways, and each decomposition must sum back to 105.76.
turnAndTalk.listenFor: A strong answer explains that each digit must land in its correct place value so the parts add back to exactly 105.76. A weak answer just says '100 and 5.76 are parts' without checking they sum correctly.
turnAndTalk.extend: Find a decomposition of 105.76 that is different from 100 + 5.76, and prove it also sums to 105.76.
extendStems: My decomposition is ___ + ___, and it equals ___.
I checked it was correct by ___.

turnAndTalk.question: You sorted 'Deon walked a shorter distance than Miguel' as something we KNOW, even without exact numbers. How can a relationship like 'shorter than' be knowledge, if we don't know the actual distance?
turnAndTalk.kernel: The Comparing Walks problem tells us Deon walked less than Miguel and Evelyn walked more than Miguel, without giving any exact distances.

stems.en: We know this because the problem states a ___, not an exact number.
stems.es: Sabemos esto porque el problema da una ___, no un número exacto.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Listen for students distinguishing between a relationship (comparison) and an exact value — a relationship is still usable information. A weak answer says we 'know nothing' because there are no numbers.
turnAndTalk.extend: Can you determine who walked the SHORTEST distance among all three students using only the relationships given? Justify your order.
extendStems: The order from shortest to longest is ___, ___, ___ because ___.
I can be sure of this order even without numbers because ___.

turnAndTalk.question: If you pick a distance for Miguel, how do you choose distances for Deon and Evelyn that stay true to the relationships in the problem?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Deon's distance must be shorter than Miguel's, and Evelyn's distance must be longer than Miguel's — any values that satisfy both relationships work.

stems.en: I picked ___ miles for Miguel, so Deon must be ___ and Evelyn must be ___.
stems.es: Elegí ___ millas para Miguel, así que Deon debe ser ___ y Evelyn debe ser ___.

stems.en: I checked my values worked by ___.
stems.es: Comprobé que mis valores funcionaban al ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: A strong answer picks a value for Miguel first, then chooses Deon's and Evelyn's values so the inequalities still hold, and explains the check. A weak answer picks three numbers with no verification against the relationships.
turnAndTalk.extend: Could two different students pick completely different sets of three distances and BOTH be correct? Explain why or why not.
extendStems: Yes/No, because the relationships only require ___.
Another valid set of distances could be ___.

turnAndTalk.question: During practice on decomposing numbers, what strategy did you use when a decomposition felt tricky?
turnAndTalk.kernel: Decomposing a number like 105.76 means breaking it into parts that must add back to the original, place value by place value.

stems.en: I knew my answer was reasonable because ___.
stems.es: Supe que mi respuesta era razonable porque ___.

turnAndTalk.listenFor: Listen for students naming a specific strategy (checking place value, adding the parts back together) rather than 'I just knew it.' A weak answer skips the verification step.
turnAndTalk.extend: How would you help a classmate who wrote 100 + 5.076 for 105.76? Use one vocabulary word.
extendStems: I would tell them to ___ because ___.
Their mistake happens when you ___ instead of ___.

questions.stem: A Ferris wheel has 10 cars. Each car holds 4 people. How many people ride at once?
questions.explanation: 10 cars of 4 people each is 10 × 4 = 40 people.
questions.stemEs: Una rueda de la fortuna tiene 10 cabinas. En cada cabina caben 4 personas. ¿Cuántas personas se suben a la vez?
choicesEs: 40 personas
14 personas
20 personas
44 personas
questions.explanationEs: 10 cabinas de 4 personas cada una es 10 × 4 = 40 personas.

questions.stem: A pizza is cut into 8 equal slices. You eat half of it. How many slices did you eat?
questions.stemEs: Una pizza está cortada en 8 rebanadas iguales. Te comes la mitad. ¿Cuántas rebanadas comiste?
choicesEs: 4 rebanadas
2 rebanadas
8 rebanadas
16 rebanadas
questions.explanationEs: La mitad de 8 rebanadas es 8 ÷ 2 = 4 rebanadas.
